title: Joining the sangat
hookLine: the code encourages visiting the gurdwara and learning Gurbani together

lines: YOU CAN'T SAY WHO TAUGHT YOU.
cards: Why does a song you've hummed alone in the car sound different in a room full of people singing it? Alone, you skip the lines you don't know.
In the room, someone beside you knows them, and you lean on their voice until you've got it. Somebody hits the high note you were afraid of. Somebody else keeps time.
By the end you know the song better, and you can't say exactly who taught you. The Sikh code has a word for that room, and it asks a Sikh not to stay home in the car.

teach.b: The word is sangat: company, the gathered congregation.

teach.h: THE WORD SINKS IN MORE DEEPLY.
teach.b: In paraphrase, the code says the Guru's word sinks in more readily and more deeply when a Sikh hears it in the sangat, and so it encourages Sikhs to visit the gurdwara and join the congregation there, to listen and to reflect on Gurbani together.
Notice what the code is claiming. Not that the gurdwara is the only place the word can be heard; a Sikh has nitnem at home, morning and night. The claim is about depth.
Some things you take in better with others in the room. Now, which room? Guru Nanak asks that himself, in Siri Rag.
In paraphrase: how is the true company known? Where the One Name alone is spoken of. That's the test.
Not the size of the hall, not who built it or who's in charge.

teach.h: KNOWN BY WHAT IS SAID THERE.
teach.b: A sangat is known by what is said there. So a crowded hall with something else at its center would fail the test, and a few people at a kitchen table reading Gurbani together would pass it.
And look at the verbs in the code: hear, reflect, learn. In a sangat one person catches a line another missed. Someone explains a word.
A child picks up a melody before she can read it. A newcomer hears a hymn for the first time in the voices of people who've loved it for years.
The learning moves sideways, from person to person, not only from the front. Not learn alone, then gather.

how: Sikhs gather in the gurdwara to hear kirtan, listen to explanations of Gurbani and join the Ardas; families often go together, and gurdwaras welcome visitors.

o: gathering with others to hear and reflect on the word
signing up as a paid member of a gurdwara
moving to live near the Golden Temple in Amritsar

p: known where the One Name is spoken
the word sinks in more deeply there

s: the code encourages Sikhs to visit the gurdwara and join the congregation
it says the Guru's word sinks in more deeply in the sangat.
in Guru Nanak's verse, the true company is known by its building
it's known by what is said there: the One Name.
the code says the gurdwara is the only place to hear Gurbani
Sikhs keep nitnem at home too. the code's claim is about depth, not the only place.

games.q: you want to understand Gurbani more deeply. where does the code point you?
o: study alone until you're sure of every line.
join the sangat and hear it with others.
wait until you've learned it all by heart.
games.why: the code encourages joining the sangat in the gurdwara, to hear and reflect together, because the word sinks in more deeply there.

practice: Bring to mind a gathering where something good is learned together, a gurdwara, which is open to visitors of any background, a study group, a table where people read aloud, and picture which day you could go and who might come with you.
If you can't go anywhere this week, picture one person to read or listen with instead.

wordCard.voice: Joining the sangat. Going to the gathered company, where the code says the Guru's word sinks in more deeply, and where Guru Nanak says the true company is known by the Name. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: learn together. The high note is easier with company. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, on joining the congregation to hear and reflect on Gurbani
